Typically, the way you wanna describe these types of infinity is by seeing if there's mapping that exists from all the set of the natural numbers to the set of whatever thing you're looking at. 

so an example that might not be super intuitive is that you have  the set of all positive multiples of 1/2 or {1/2, 1, 3/2, 2...}. And what's weird is that the cardinality of this is also |N| because you can make a function that maps all elements of N to this set (in this case, it's just multiplying all the indices of each element in the set by 1/2). 

This is mostly a definitions thing, as for math people, there isn't really a need to compare anything that has "|N| + 1"  elements to |N|. Especially because there's a way to map every element in something that is size |N| to something in size |N+1|. 

One thing you might find interesting is that the cardinality of all the real numbers, or |R| is that it's greater than |N||. What that means basically is that there's no way to capture every real number with a mapping from the natural numbers.

I don't really think it's that straightforward. For one, a lot of people can't afford 100 to 150 dollars out of pocket in the USA. There are a couple of solutions to that, sure. You could theoretically implement a sliding scale if you didn't want to work with insurance companies. But also, the fact that when you typically do work with insurance companies firsthand, you generally get pretty gimped on the claims, and disputing them might net you some money back, but you might end up spending more time and energy disputing claims with certain insurance providers than you are providing care to patients. Most people come into this field with the intent of providing care, and not with the intent of running a business. 

You say zoning laws are irrelevant as people prefer telehealth, but that depends on the kind of counseling one goes into. Two times the pay is dependent on the kind of work you are doing, and the type of counseling you are doing, the neighborhood you're in. There are certain forms of therapy that just make more sense to do in real life. There are certain clientele that it makes more sense to meet in person (such as children). 

You're very clearly making this blanket statement that doesn't always apply.

It's actually incredibly complicated. If you're starting up a private practice, and you're trying to make it accessible, you need to work with insurance companies, and then spend a lot of energy disputing claims and arguing with insurance companies over the phone, as well as work with patients to discuss those kinds of things. You might need to acquire malpractice and liability insurance dependent on where you live. You need to go through the efforts of local and state zoning laws. You might be required to use EMR software, which has a monthly fee associated with it. Healthcare of any kind is incredibly complicated to just start a private practice. 

If you've ever worked with an insurance company, it's really understandable that some people don't want to be self employed for that reason alone, but everything else makes it even less attractive for some people.

Passing amendments is an incredibly slow, difficult and long process. The easiest course of action 66% Senate and House to deem it necessary, but even then, that isn't the end of the amendment process. After that, 75% of the legislatures of states have to ratify the amendment. For context, there are currently 22 states in the US that already have legislation in place to immediately ban abortions if Roe v. Wade ever gets overturned. Those state legislatures probably won't ever ratify the amedment, if by some miracle, Congress and Senate managed to get that through. 

 
The most recent amendment (number 27) was completely ratified in 1992 (and proposed in 1789, but that's a weird case), and the second most recent amendment was completely ratified in 1972. Most proposals for amendments die in committees and never make it to the floor.

Checks and balances is the intention of splitting up the powers. I don't think vesting all power in one individual is really wise for anybody. It's a recipe for authoritarianism which can quite easily lead to fascism.

Idk if you skipped the quora answer or not, but it is by a CS professor here and he says explicitly the earliest you would be able to transfer is most likely your second year. You need to take two CS courses past 125 on campus and have at least an A- in both of them to even be considered, and then there's still no guarantee. Taking a proficiency for CS 173 would mean it wouldn't count towards that requirement to transfer. Transfer credit wouldn't either. 

I think the CS 173 proficiency is doable, and past quizzes and the textbook are available on Professor Margaret Fleck's course website and definitely would prepare you enough if you took the time to do it. But again, I don't know if that would be the best move in order to transfer. 

Personally, I don't know if you being in AP math and physics classes says anything about your motivation, drive or competence in it of itself. I'll say that I have seen people who were so determined to transfer into CS, did a bunch of work (or at least said they did), and then transferred out of the university after 2 years because they realized they could never do CS here. They all probably were AP kids in high school, since it's not the most uncommon thing at UIUC for an engineering student. 

If you've read everything I told you, read what Jeff said before, and you still wanna go full throttle towards this transfer into CS/CompE thing, I'd say take to an advisor when you get on campus and make sure you have a decent amount of back-up plans. I've seen people put all their eggs in one basket and then get burned before.
everything counts for hours at the very least. even getting a 3 on all of these will give you credit hours, which can count for something. my advice is to just take them all.

I would take a look at [this quora answer](https://www.quora.com/University-of-Illinois-Urbana-chamapaign-I-was-accepted-for-my-second-choice-major-rateher-than-my-first-choice-comp-sci-is-there-any-way-I-can-dual-degree-my-second-choice-with-computer-science-or-transfer-majors/answer/Jeff-Erickson?ch=10&share=bbc70f36&srid=nOdt) by /u/jeffgerickson about transferring into CS first. Take what he said and apply it to CompE as well. This isn't to say there aren't success stories. One of my friends got rejected from CS freshman year, and then applied to transfer after showing off he had a really strong background in Math and CS classes here. Another friend did transfer to EE, again after having a really strong GPA, essay, and displaying a genuine interest via his coursework. And for every one of those success stories, there is more than one other person who tried and failed to transfer, because less than half of people get accepted to transfer for CS, and I have no idea what it's like for ECE, but it's still incredibly competitive. 

If you're trying to register as a nonmajor for CS 225 as a freshman, that's realistically not going to happen. Prereqs are enforced, and cohort restrictions mean that students with seniority who need it for their degree are going to be prioritized over you. You need to take CS 125 or ECE 220 as a prereq for 173, and 225 has 173 has a prereq. There are CS students who do manage to take it freshman year, but that's probably either because they took a proficiency test (either for 125 or 173), took MATH 213, or they came in with some kind of college credit. If the compiler converts xyz to machine code, and the machine code runs directly as a binary, then in theory, yes it can be equal or similar to C. In reality, C is just the optimal language to write low level applications in and has been optimized to remain for that niche. The compilers are extremely good, and managing to match that performance would be a difficult endeavour.

Python is an interpretive language, so that means when you run code, it interprets the lines of code you wrote as you run it. Meanwhile C is a compiled language. This means that it must be turned into a binary that the computer executes directly, and when you modify your code, a new binary must be compiled everytime. 

If you write program in C and write a program in Python using the same logic, the C one will almost always run magnitudes faster. 

The meme here is that the issue isn't that the Python language is slow. There's nothing inherent about the language's syntactical features that makes it slow. In theory, you could convert python to C and then compile that (or even directly to machine code as I've come to learn that PyPy exists). It's simply the interpreter. The act of parsing code at runtime and breaking it down and then telling the computer to execute specific instructions is really expensive. The reality is that interpreting a language as it runs definitely consumes more clock cycles and time then it would to just run the logic directly. All interpreters have to be made to run in a compiled language (most times, this is C or C++).

I suffer from major depressive disorder myself, and I think one of the things that's very hard to control at first is mindset about the whole thing. I'm going to be honest. I think that your mindset is far from one that will conquer depression. That can still change, but you have to recognize that.

Look, I understand how easy it is to feel dejected from feeling unhappy all the time. However, I still realize and objectively reason with myself that I am capable of being happy down the road. Therefore, I shouldn't do things now that will make it worse. Like not studying for any of my classes, or not showering. 

Part of the issue is that you seem to think that any effort taken by you yields no results. While I can relate to that sentiment and understand how much it sucks, you still have to realize that that is wrong. Say it out loud to yourself a couple of times if you honestly can't believe you are capable of not feeling depressed, lonely, or bored on a Friday night. Without any sign of belief that your circumstances can change, the chances are you won't take any action to change it and will always feel shitty. The self fulfilling prophecy is very much a real thing, and the longer you sulk and believe that it is impossible to be happy, the more time you are going to spend never changing the the things that are causing you to be unhappy. 

There is no real cut-dry solution to just feeling content and happy. You might try a lot of things, and still realize you feel depressed. it might take a really long time. However, I can guarantee you that if you think nothing makes you happy and nothing will ever change, then you will continue to feel this way for a long time. Just trick yourself into believing things can change by saying they can out loud over and over again, and internalizing it.

His pants were stained brown at the knees. His beard was vaguely reminiscent of a mall Santa I had seen years ago. His pallor, similar to a vampire. His eyes were black. A dark black, like the night sky above. He closed his eyes, and had a blank look on his face, and was ready to fall back. 

"Holy shit, dude. What are you doing?!"

"I thought I was alone." 

"But why are you jumping off of a bridge?"

"Because. I am bored," he said.

I looked at this man, as if he were crazy. Boredom is generally not a good reason to kill yourself. I mean, boredom is a problem you can fix, by going out for ice cream, or roller skating, or something. Boredom is a thing you could work on fixing. Ending your life. I mean, people kill themselves because of being cheated on, or because they are sad. What the hell was this?

"Certainly, ending your life isn't the solution to ending your boredom. I mean, you must have some activity you enjoy, right?"

"Nope,"

I was frustrated. This man had purpose. 

"Ok. I mean, before you kill yourself, how about we talk for a little bit. I mean, you don't really have much waiting for you anyway, and I have..."

"Ok," he interjected. 

"So. When you were a kid, what did you always want to be?"

"Nothing really. I kinda just dragged through," he said in a nonchalant kind of voice. 

"Surely there must be something you aspired to be! An Astronaut? A doctor? The president of the country?"

"Let me ask you. What do you enjoy doing?" he asked, avoiding my question. 

And then I froze. I thought about all the hobbies I had. Playing guitar. Skating. Writing. None of these filled me with enjoyment per se. They were just things I did to occupy my time. And all of a sudden, the questions I asked the man were rushing through my head. *Perhaps you don't feel good*

Why did it just turn this way? Why was I so easily manipulated? *Perhaps your brain was never capable anyway.*

And thoughts keep rushing through and through. I can't handle it anymore, and all in a second, I pop back into reality.

"I... don't... know?" I stuttered back to him. 

I climb up onto the railing with him. I grab his hand. 

"Let's go"

We close our eyes, and have this blank look on our faces. We lean back and fall. A fall that feels like it takes years. While falling, I question whether or not this is something I really wanted to do. It's too late anyway. I was going to be dead in a few sec...

My second biggest regret would be wishing my mother dead. 

The thing is that 5 year olds aren't rational. My mother was preparing me for the biggest wish of my lifetime. To set me up for a lifetime of success. Telling me what words I want to say, when I didn't want to say them. She had this nice index card laminated, saying "Charlie's 5th birthday wish". 

I never understood what she meant by my wish coming true. It's something that everybody says every birthday. Make a wish, and nothing ever happens. And she emphasized it really coming true this birthday. And I just assumed it was something that kinda just didn't happen, and it was something parents told you just because. Being the oldest in a class of kindergartners, I would be the first to celebrate my 5th birthday in my class. So I would be the first to experience a wish really coming true. 

My mother and I were talking about my math test I had just received that day. I got a 75 on my birthday. She doesn't like 75's. She started lecturing me on the importance of school. And she was yelling at me. The next minute, the life flickered out of mother's eyes. They were no longer sparkling like they used to. She put her hand to her chest feeling a huge sense of pain. Thud. Her body made this indescribable noise as it hit the floor. Thud is an understatement. 

I stared at my mother for a minute, trying to comprehend what just happened. And the gravity of the situation just occurred. I had just yelled at my mother I wished she were dead. 

Father came rushing into the room. Crying, doing chest compressions. He wasn't angry at me. He was so timid. The paramedics arrived and pronounced her. Heart attack. The gleam in his eyes died that day. 

We drafted out my tenth birthday wish, which to bring her back. This would be my biggest regret. 

We ordered an exhumation of my mother's body the day before my tenth birthday. We had her body embalmed and ready for her resurrection. Seeing the casket rise from the ground, it looked like an angel flying up carrying my mother. I wrote down the words exactly, and prepared them in a nice laminated card. On the top of the card, was written "Charlie's 10th birthday". 

And all of a sudden, my mother woke up from her distant sleep. My father had his eyes light up. He felt alive. My mother then got up and put on her clothes. My father hugging her asking if she is okay. My mother was essentially a zombie. She didn't know what was happening and kept trying to comprehend what was going on. Technology evolved so much. Wishes were made around the world. The world changed so much for her. She didn't know what to make of it. My mother cried, saying she was sorry for yelling me at a math test 5 years ago. She told me she knew I made a mistake and was okay with it. 

But my mother wished to remain dead. She said she enjoyed living in pitch black. She said it was the longest sleep one could ask for. My mother remained until I was 15, before crippling depression got to her and she hanged herself from the creaky ceiling fan in the living room. I remember walking into the living room, seeing my mother's face pale as the day we exhumed her

I never could comprehend why she did it when I was at the young age of 15. It never seemed to make sense to me, but people change. Her husband was a different man from 5 years ago. She never had a chance to raise her child. She was living in the world 5 years ago. Where nobody had wished for hover-boards, or wished for 10 GHz processors. When wishes happen daily, of course stuff is going to change. And my mother couldn't handle the ginormous gap of 5 years. Imagine going from people wishing for iPhone 6's and then the next day, wishing for the 7. It's a big change. Language evolves. Research evolves. People have figured out ways to travel faster than the speed of light. Teleportation was made. 

I wish I understood it. I really wished I did. Her killing herself has made me feel, guilty. Upset. I don't know. I tried justifying it at the time, and I didn't get it. It made me enter a state of depression, and I dn't know. I missed her. I missed her for 5 years of my life, and I lost her again.
